title: Quantum Computing's Real Metric: Compute Per Watt Over Qubit Count - News and Statistics
excerpt: Quantum computing needs a new yardstick: compute per watt. As energy becomes the bottleneck, measuring useful output per unit of power and cost matters more than raw qubit counts.
content:
Oct 27, 2026

Quantum Computing Must Measure Compute Per Watt, not Just Qubits

According to projections from UN researchers, data centers in 2030 will require double the electricity and water they consumed in 2025, with AI as the primary driver. Energy has emerged as a critical limiting factor for expanding compute capacity, and quantum computing faces the same pressure even though its advancement is still commonly measured through raw qubit counts and fidelity rates.

Such metrics are important, yet alone they cannot show how much genuinely useful processing capability a system provides. The fundamental objective is to advance technology toward a practical scale, which in the simplest terms demands that the value generated per solution surpass the expense per solution.

Quantum machines offer genuine potential for practical applications, from speeding up pharmaceutical development and materials science to enabling more efficient machine learning once they reach a useful scale. Attaining that milestone requires taking operational costs as seriously as the underlying physics, and a clearer grasp of useful compute output per unit of energy or expenditure is essential to that goal.

Power as the denominator

The calculation has two components. Power sits in the denominator: cryogenic cooling and control electronics consume electricity continuously, and large-scale quantum systems will draw tens of megawatts. Since quantum computation can grow exponentially with processor size, the numerator carries greater weight. The critical factor is how much compute power a system produces for every watt it draws, which depends on the QPU architecture.

Classical computing encountered similar challenges. Processors were long evaluated by clock frequency, but as data centers expanded, power became the constraint and performance per watt became the decisive measure. Since 2007, the Green500 has ranked supercomputers by computations per watt alongside the TOP500 ranking by raw speed.

Lessons from the AI buildout

With the rise of AI and hyperscale compute expansion, demand keeps exceeding supply. The industry has spent years catching up, retrofitting power and cooling rather than planning for them from the outset. Operators now resort to on-site gas generators for new data centers, which marks a regression. For quantum, the argument is that an energy-efficient architecture should be established before reaching that same turning point.

A superior benchmark is therefore needed, with compute-per-watt as the central metric: the useful computation obtained for each watt consumed. This approach compels buyers and builders to weigh output against the energy that produced it instead of counting qubits and assuming everything else follows.

The metric tallies power drawn by cooling, control electronics and classical computing on one side, and useful quantum computation delivered on the other. If buyers and builders embrace compute-per-watt as a shared standard, the industry will optimize for the useful processing power extracted from each unit of energy. The same reasoning extends to cost, with compute-per-dollar weighing output against what a system costs to build and operate.

Scaling up versus scaling out

Achieving more compute per watt depends largely on chip design. On the power side, chip and system architecture choices determine how much electricity is needed for cryogenics, control hardware and classical compute.

On the compute side, architectural differences are far greater. Two primary scaling strategies exist: scaling up and scaling out. Scaling out involves networking existing QPUs together to expand a quantum computer, while scaling up means surmounting current scaling bottlenecks and enlarging the QPU itself. Both approaches increase qubit count, but increasing qubit count differs from increasing compute power.

A recent study quantifies this, demonstrating that quantum computers built around large QPUs generate up to exponentially more compute power than a networked quantum computer. Network links explain the gap, being considerably slower and more lossy than connections inside a single QPU.

This networking penalty is frequently overlooked in industry discussions about scaling quantum computers, yet it can determine whether a workload runs for one hour on 100,000 qubits or for 10 years on 100 billion qubits. Networking will matter, but later; the argument holds that the industry must first scale up, then scale out.

The architecture and manufacturing processes for these systems are being determined now, and those choices set the trajectory for the coming decade. Quantum is at an earlier stage than AI, so the industry retains a choice AI lacked: begin measuring progress in a way that accounts for economics and power usage today, or face the consequences of neglecting those considerations.
